912: (18) The ilpas and the pot that were removed from the fire while fully boiling — if they are not fully cooked one may not stir them even with a spoon, since this is like cooking. And if they are fully cooked, even though one may not stir the pot, one may stir something that is fully cooked. But wool in a cauldron — even after it is fully colored one may not stir it because of dyeing. {Rama: And l'chatchila one should not stir even in a fully cooked item with a ladle; and the world has the practice of permitting types of legumes that are taken out with a spoon since it is impossible otherwise.}
915: (22) 'But wool, etc.' — for in this case there is dyeing. Alternatively the wool requires a lot of cooking, so wrote the Rosh.
917: (23) 'Even in a pot, etc.' — there the Mahariv wrote that one should not pour even a spoonful of water into it because it cooks, as stated in the first chapter of Shabbos regarding an upright cauldron smeared with clay.
921: (44) 'And l'chatchila, etc.' — and the world has the practice of permitting types of legumes that are taken out with a spoon since it is impossible otherwise, and they have those to rely upon — see what was written in siman 253 seif 4.
923: (40) 'Forbidden' — for in this there is the concern of dyeing.
925: (41) 'And l'chatchila, etc.' — and the world has the practice of permitting types of legumes taken out with a spoon since it is impossible otherwise, and they have those to rely upon — see siman 253.
927: (53) 'Seif 18, if not' — as written in seif 4.
929: (54) 'And if' — then there is no concern of cooking, since returning is permitted, as stated in the Tosefta above.
933: (56) 'Even though' — and so it is proven in the Jerusalem Talmud — Ran. That is why they left it unattributed in the Mishnah and Beit Hillel permits, and they did not distinguish between upright and smeared.
935: (113) 'That they were removed while fully boiling' — he specified 'removed' to teach us the novel point that even in this case it is forbidden when they are not fully cooked. And when they are fully cooked, even if standing on the fire it is permitted to stir as stated in seif 4.
937: (114) 'That is found stirring, etc.' — for stirring the pot is a real prohibition, and one who stirs is liable to a chatas according to what the Shulchan Aruch ruled above in seif 4: that in this he assists and hastens the cooking.
939: (115) 'All its consumption is permitted' — even to stir in it, since there is no cooking after cooking, as stated above in seif 4.
941: (116) 'Forbidden to stir in it' — because of dyeing, for the act of dyeing is always to stir so that it does not scorch; and through stirring the dye is absorbed into the wool more.
943: (117) 'Even in a pot, etc.' — rather, he should overturn the pot into a bowl and not take out with a spoon. And see the later authorities who say the practice is not to be stringent in this.
946: 'Even in a pot, etc.' — see the Mishna Berurah in the name of the later authorities — and they are the Taz, the Eliyah Rabbah, the Chayei Adam, and the Gra. And the later authorities conclude that b'dieved one should not forbid.
949: (104) Introduction to the seif — part of the cooking process is stirring; therefore stirring an uncooked dish that is on the fire constitutes a Torah-level prohibition of cooking. And also stirring wool in a cauldron of dye — even after the dye has been absorbed, it is forbidden to stir it on Shabbos because of the prohibition of dyeing.
951: (105) 'Because of cooking' — meaning: mixing the food hastens the cooking, and is therefore forbidden by Torah law.
953: (106) 'Permitted' — since there is no cooking after cooking. And even if it is mitzamek v'yafeh lo, meaning continued cooking improves the food.
955: (107) 'Wool into a cauldron' — meaning: when it is not a pot with food, but a pot in which wool is heated with dye so that the wool will become dyed. And to do so on Shabbos is forbidden by Torah law because of the melacha of dyeing.
957: (108) 'Forbidden to stir in it' — in the melacha of dyeing there is no permission to dye after the color has been absorbed, rather as long as the wool is in the cauldron any stirring constitutes dyeing.
959: (109) 'In any case' — even if the dish is cooked, since they fear that perhaps the food was not fully cooked. The answer is to overturn the pot into a bowl, and to take out with a spoon only for legumes since there is no other way.
